findings.element: state=print and state=phone (opened) — .b-behindCount ("3 moments") against the .b-behindNote written at render-b.js:384 with data-when="listed"/"open" ("2 moments behind you, and one thing that did not happen.")
findings.problem: One block, one noun, two totals. Driven at 1440 on ?state=print the head reads "Behind you · 3 moments" at y=562 and 226px below it, on the same sheet, the closing line reads "2 moments behind you, and one thing that did not happen." Three rows are printed between them. On ?state=phone the same pair appears the moment the disclosure is opened, under a summary that still says 3. Both numbers are defensible under different definitions of "moment" — the head counts past.length, the sentence counts done.length — but the reader is not given the definitions, only the word, twice, with different numbers attached. This is the self-contradicting-count class from the defect library and it is now sitting on the one artifact that cannot be corrected after it exists: a guest holding the printed sheet is being asked to decide which of the product's two counts of the same three rows to believe. Everywhere the rows are listed the sentence is also pure restatement — each row already carries its own "Not going ahead" label ten pixels above the sentence that announces it.
findings.fix: The block gets one count and one writer. Keep .b-behindCount as the only number: past.length + " moments", derived as it is now. Then strip the count out of the note at render-b.js:384 so it never states a second total: where dropped.length is 0 render nothing at all (the listed rows already carry their own state, so the sentence has no fact left to add), and where dropped.length is 1 render exactly "One of them did not happen." Leave the folded note at line 383 alone — "2 done, the last of them 18 April. One thing is not going ahead." partitions the head's 3 rather than contradicting it, which is the behaviour the listed note should copy.

findings.element: .b-who on every guest surface — state=phone, desk, print, ended, loading (h1.b-who "Mara & Finn")
findings.problem: On the screen the whole company is judged by, the couple's own names are the smallest and faintest ink on the page. Measured at 390 the h1 renders 12px/400 at rgba(255,255,255,0.62) — identical in size, weight and alpha to "days", "Today is 16 July", "Kept by Orla" and "Updated 15 July 2026" — while the machine's number above it runs 96px at full ink, and 148px on the A4 keepsake against the same 12px name. The one genuinely owner-written string in the block is set at the ladder step reserved for stamps and units, so the artifact reads as a countdown widget carrying a wedding's name rather than as a wedding that happens to carry a count. The panel's own round-3 refuter closed a different finding with the words "the lever is the .b-who treatment, which is the only genuinely owner-written string in the block", and the lever has not been pulled in three rounds. The defect library states the rule directly: a person's words outrank the machine's.
findings.fix: Move .b-who one step up the declared size ladder on the guest surfaces (phone, desk, print, ended, loading) — from --size-label to the next declared step — and take it to full --fore ink rather than the 0.62 stamp alpha, keeping weight 400 and its existing tracking role so nothing else on the ladder moves. Leave the count, .b-when and .b-sub exactly as they are: the descent 79 → Saturday 3 October 2026 → Wedding day stays intact, and this only lifts the names out of the footer register they currently share with the version stamp.

findings.element: foot() at render-b.js:428 — "Kept by Orla", rendered 11px/400 at 0.62 alpha beside "Updated 15 July 2026" and "Signal Timeline" on phone, desk and print
findings.problem: The person who made and sent the plan appears once, in the last line, in the same type, ink and row as a version stamp and the vendor name. A guest who opens this on a phone meets a number, a date, a rail of seven rows and a footer credit, and the only human agency on the artifact is filed as metadata between a timestamp and a logo. The round-3 refuter that killed the sender's-voice finding endorsed this remedy explicitly — "promote the real F.workspace.owner out of foot() into the hero region of phone, desk and print as the mono micro attribution, and leave the footer stamp alone" — and it was not done in rounds 4 or 5. It needs no fixture field, no invented sentence and no new noun; the string already renders.
findings.fix: Render the existing F.workspace.owner attribution in the hero region of ?state=phone, ?state=desk and ?state=print, directly under .b-who, at --size-label in the mono face at 0.62 alpha, using the string foot() already composes: "Kept by Orla". Remove that one span from foot() on those three states so the name is stated once, and leave "Updated 15 July 2026" and "Signal Timeline" in the footer untouched.

findings.element: state=print — .b-unit ("days away on Thursday 16 July 2026", y=269) and .b-origin ("Today, Thursday 16 July 2026", y=176)
findings.problem: The same twenty-four-character date is printed twice on one sheet of A4, in the same face at the same 11px size, once as the qualifier on the count and once as the origin tick of the rail. Round 5's dating fix is what created it: .b-origin used to read "Today, 16 July" and now carries the full weekday date, so two related statements have become a verbatim repeat across the sheet's two columns. Round 4's refuter had already written the fix — "shorten .b-origin to bare 'Today' beside its tick, since the date is already stated above it" — and accepted it as the lever if the pairing ever read flat. On paper it reads flat: the sheet states today twice before it states anything about the wedding.
findings.fix: On the print state only, set .b-origin to the single word "Today". The count's qualifier .b-unit keeps the full "days away on Thursday 16 July 2026", which is the sentence that has to survive being read months later; the rail tick only has to name its own zero. Screen states keep "Today, 16 July" as they are.

findings.element: state=publish — .b-pressBody at render-b.js:1276, "It carries the day, the distance and the plan, and nothing from your workspace: no notes, no suppliers, no prices."
findings.problem: This is the owner's most consequential sentence — the one that decides whether she trusts the product with someone else's wedding — and it is the only place in the product where a user reads the word "workspace". Every other string names things the way the interface does: the plan, the day, the moments, The Orchard, Mara & Finn. The container being referred to is displayed 100px above as "The Orchard, events" and is never once called a workspace on screen, so the sentence introduces a piece of software vocabulary at the exact moment it is asking to be believed about what stays private. It is the single SaaS noun in an otherwise entirely plain vocabulary, and it is the one Home, Notes and Tasks would inherit.
findings.fix: Compose the sentence from the name already on screen: "It carries the day, the distance and the plan, and nothing else from " + F.workspace.name + ": no notes, no suppliers, no prices." — rendering as "...and nothing else from The Orchard, events: no notes, no suppliers, no prices." Same length, same claim, no new noun, and it points at the thing the owner can see rather than at a category she has never been shown.

biggestWin: The win is that the owner's voice is now genuinely at the benchmark — "When is the day? / Everything on this page is measured from it, so it is the only thing needed to start.", "This is as far as it goes. Wedding day is the last day.", "Nothing has been deleted. Only the link stopped working." and every undo sentence are declarative, concrete and unhedged, and would sit unaltered inside Stripe or Linear. The single thing holding this seat below 9.5 is that nothing a guest reads was written by a human: the couple's names are set at stamp size and stamp ink, the sender is a footer credit beside a version number, and every sentence on the received artifact is machine-composed from dates — so the most emotional surface in the suite currently reads as a very well-written instrument rather than as something one person handed another. Two thirds of that is polish and is costed above (.b-who up one ladder step, the attribution out of the footer, roughly half a day). The last third is a build, not a decision and not polish: a publish-time note field carried through the audience DTO and shown on phone, desk and print, with the empty case rendering nothing at all rather than a placeholder — roughly two days including moderation, and it must ship with a genuinely captured sentence, never with lab-written copy standing in for one.
